title: House Robber III
notes:
Task and constraints: Maximize the sum of selected tree-node values without selecting a node and its direct child; every node can be solved once.
Idea: dfs returns (take, skip). For a node, take adds its value to both children's skip scores; skip adds the larger take-or-skip score from each child. The root returns the larger score.
Technique and why it applies: Tree DP separates the two decisions at each node, so a parent's choice determines which child states are allowed.
Invariant: For each subtree, take is the best score when its root is selected and skip is the best when its root is excluded.
Edge cases: A null node returns (0,0); a leaf compares its value against zero; negative-valued nodes can be skipped when doing so improves the total. Recursion depth follows tree height.
Complexity: Each node is visited once for O(n) time; recursive calls use O(h) stack space for tree height h.
complexity_reason: Each node is processed once and returns two scores; recursion stores call frames along a root-to-leaf path of height h.

title: House Robber III
notes:
Task and constraints: Choose tree nodes for maximum total value without selecting both a node and its direct child; the recursive method computes two scores per subtree.
Idea: dfs returns an int array where index 0 is take and index 1 is skip. Taking n adds n.val to both child skip scores; skipping n adds the maximum score from each child.
Technique and why it applies: Two-state tree DP captures the parent-child restriction locally and combines independent left and right subtree optima.
Invariant: For every returned array, its first entry is optimal with that subtree root selected and its second is optimal with the root omitted.
Edge cases: A null node returns two zeros; a leaf's take score is its value and skip is zero; recursion depth may overflow the Java call stack for a highly skewed tree.
Complexity: Each node is visited once, giving O(n) time; recursion requires O(h) stack space, aside from small arrays returned per call.
complexity_reason: The recursion visits each node once and retains call frames proportional to tree height; each call creates a two-element result array.

title: Counting Bits
notes:
Task and constraints: Return an array giving the number of set bits for every integer from 0 through n; the output itself requires O(n) space.
Idea: dp is initialized to n+1 zeros. For each positive i, dp[i] is set to dp[i>>1] plus the low bit i&1, using the already-computed count for its half.
Technique and why it applies: Dynamic programming on the right shift reuses the bit count of floor(i/2), then adds one exactly when i is odd.
Invariant: Before processing i, dp[j] is correct for every j<i, so dp[i>>1] is available and dp[i] becomes the population count of i.
Edge cases: n=0 returns [0]; i=1 gets one from dp[0]+1; even numbers add zero and odd numbers add one. The loop is skipped for n=0.
Complexity: One constant-work update for each i gives O(n) time and the returned dp array occupies O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The loop fills one array entry per integer from 1 to n, and the output array stores n+1 counts.

title: Counting Bits
notes:
Task and constraints: Produce bit counts for all integers in [0,n], returning an int array of length n+1.
Idea: bits defaults to zero at index zero. For each i from 1 to n, bits[i] equals bits[i>>1] plus the least significant bit i&1.
Technique and why it applies: The recurrence removes the low bit by shifting right, so the count for i is the count for floor(i/2) plus one when i is odd.
Invariant: Every index smaller than i has already been computed correctly, including i>>1, allowing the current count to be built from a solved state.
Edge cases: n=0 returns a one-element array containing zero; i=1 produces one; the loop bound i<=n includes n and avoids reading beyond the array. Very large n is limited by array memory.
Complexity: The loop runs n times for O(n) time; bits contains n+1 integers, using O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The method fills n array entries after initialization and returns an array of n+1 integers.

title: Flatten Nested List Iterator
notes:
Task and constraints: Implement left-to-right iteration over arbitrarily nested lists, returning only integers and expanding nested lists lazily when needed.
Idea: The constructor reverses the top-level list into self.stack. hasNext repeatedly expands a top nested list by popping it and pushing its children in reverse; next calls hasNext, raises StopIteration if exhausted, and otherwise pops an integer.
Technique and why it applies: An explicit LIFO stack simulates depth-first traversal while reversed pushes preserve the original left-to-right order.
Invariant: After hasNext returns true, the stack top is the next integer in traversal order; all nested lists above that integer have been expanded.
Edge cases: An empty input immediately reports no next item; deeply nested single-child lists are expanded until an integer appears; calling next after exhaustion raises StopIteration.
Complexity: Each nested value is pushed and popped a bounded number of times, giving O(1) amortized work per returned integer; stack storage is O(d+n) for nesting depth d and pending values.
complexity_reason: Each nested value is expanded or returned once, and the explicit stack stores pending values across the nested structure.

title: Flatten Nested List Iterator
notes:
Task: Implement next/hasNext over nested lists while preserving integer order.
Idea: Use a deque as a stack and expand the front nested list until an integer is at the front.
Invariant: The deque front is always the next unconsumed nested item in traversal order.
Edge cases: Empty inner lists are removed during hasNext; NestedInteger is supplied by the judge.
complexity_reason: Every nested item is expanded or returned once; the deque stores pending values.

title: Power of Four
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether n is a positive exact power of four; the code uses bit operations rather than repeatedly dividing by four.
Idea: It first rejects n<=0, then requires n&(n-1) to be zero so exactly one bit is set, and finally checks that the bit overlaps mask 0x55555555.
Technique and why it applies: A power of four has one set bit at an even bit position; the single-bit test excludes other bit patterns and the mask excludes powers of two at odd positions.
Invariant: The conjunction accepts only positive integers with one set bit in a position selected by the alternating-bit mask.
Edge cases: 1 is accepted; 4 is accepted because bit 2 is in the mask; 2 and 8 are rejected because their only set bit is in an odd position, and zero is rejected before bit tests matter.
Complexity: A fixed number of integer comparisons and bitwise operations gives O(1) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: The method evaluates a fixed sequence of positivity, single-bit, and mask tests and allocates no additional structures.

title: Power of Four
notes:
Task and constraints: Check whether positive int n is a power of four using constant-time bit tests.
Idea: The method rejects nonpositive values, checks (n&(n-1))==0 for exactly one set bit, and checks intersection with 0x55555555 to require that bit at an even position.
Technique and why it applies: Binary powers of four have a single 1 bit in positions 0, 2, 4, and so on; the mask selects exactly those positions in a positive 32-bit int.
Invariant: A true result means n is positive, has only one set bit, and that bit belongs to the even-position mask.
Edge cases: n=1 and n=4 return true; n=2 and n=8 return false due to the mask; n=0 short-circuits before any further checks. Java int bitwise operations preserve the intended low 32-bit representation.
Complexity: Only a fixed number of comparisons and bitwise operations are performed, so time and auxiliary space are O(1).
complexity_reason: The method performs a constant number of primitive int operations and creates no extra data structures.

title: Integer Break
notes:
Task and constraints: Split integer n into at least two positive parts to maximize their product; the loop repeatedly removes a factor of three while leaving a final remainder.
Idea: For n<=3 the method returns n-1. Otherwise product starts at one; while n>4 it multiplies product by three and subtracts three from n, then multiplies by the remaining n.
Technique and why it applies: The greedy decomposition favors parts of three for maximum product, but leaves a remainder of four intact because 2×2 is better than 3×1.
Invariant: After each loop iteration, product is the product of removed threes and n is the unprocessed remainder; termination leaves n in {2,3,4}.
Edge cases: n=2 returns 1; n=4 bypasses the loop and returns 4; n=5 removes one three and returns 6. Python integers expand as needed for large products.
Complexity: The loop performs about n/3 iterations, so the supplied time label is O(n); only product and n are stored, giving O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Each iteration subtracts three until the remainder is at most four, with only product and n held as scalar state.

title: Integer Break
notes:
Task and constraints: Partition n into at least two positive integers and maximize their product; the implementation repeatedly factors out threes until the remainder is at most four.
Idea: Values n<=3 return n-1. Otherwise product accumulates factors of three while n>4; the final return multiplies product by the remaining n.
Technique and why it applies: Greedy splitting into threes maximizes product for larger n, while retaining a remainder of four avoids replacing 2+2 with 3+1.
Invariant: product equals the product of all extracted threes and n is the remaining amount; on loop exit n is two, three, or four.
Edge cases: n=2 returns 1; n=4 returns 4 without entering the loop; n=5 returns 6 after extracting one three. Java int multiplication can overflow if inputs exceed the problem's constraints, so correctness relies on the stated bound.
Complexity: The loop runs O(n) iterations under the supplied label and uses O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The loop repeatedly subtracts three and multiplies a scalar accumulator; no input-sized structure is created.

title: Reverse String
notes:
Task and constraints: Reverse a character list in place using constant extra space; only symmetric positions need to be swapped.
Idea: left starts at index zero and right at the final index. While left<right, the tuple assignment swaps their characters, then both indices move inward.
Technique and why it applies: Two pointers exchange mirrored positions, reversing the sequence without building a second list.
Invariant: Before each swap, positions outside the interval [left,right] are already in their final reversed positions; the unprocessed interval remains to be handled symmetrically.
Edge cases: Empty and one-character lists skip the loop; an even-length list swaps all pairs; an odd-length list leaves its middle character untouched. The function mutates s and returns None.
Complexity: Each pair is swapped once, giving O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
complexity_reason: The two indices move inward once per pair and the swaps occur directly in the input list.

title: Reverse String
notes:
Task and constraints: Reverse a char array in place with constant auxiliary space; the method does not return a replacement array.
Idea: l begins at zero and r at s.length-1. While l<r, a temporary char saves s[l], the endpoints are exchanged, and both pointers move inward.
Technique and why it applies: Symmetric two-pointer swapping places each character at its mirror index without allocating a second array.
Invariant: Every index outside the current [l,r] interval already contains its final reversed character; only the central interval remains unsolved.
Edge cases: Empty and singleton arrays require no swaps; odd-length arrays keep their middle char; indexing is safe because the loop stops when l>=r. The input array itself is mutated.
Complexity: There are at most floor(n/2) swaps, so time is O(n) and extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: The loop performs at most half as many swaps as array elements and uses one temporary char.

title: Reverse Vowels of a String
notes:
Task and constraints: Reverse only the vowels in a string, preserving every consonant and its position; the method returns a new string.
Idea: The code copies s to chars, then moves l rightward until it finds a vowel and r leftward until it finds a vowel. It swaps those two characters, advances both pointers, and joins chars at the end.
Technique and why it applies: Two-pointer scanning pairs the leftmost remaining vowel with the rightmost remaining vowel, which reverses the vowel subsequence without moving consonants.
Invariant: All characters outside [l,r] have already been finalized, and the vowels swapped so far occupy reversed positions relative to the original vowel order.
Edge cases: A string with no vowels remains unchanged; a single vowel needs no effective swap; uppercase vowels are included by the explicit set. Empty input returns an empty string.
Complexity: The scans visit each character at most a constant number of times, giving O(n) time; chars and the result require O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The pointers scan the character array inward once, while the mutable character list and returned string use linear space.

title: Reverse Vowels of a String
notes:
Task and constraints: Return a string with vowels reversed while non-vowels stay at their original indices; both lowercase and uppercase English vowels count.
Idea: The method converts s to char array a. Nested while loops advance l and r to vowels, then a temporary char swaps them; the pointers continue until they meet, and new String(a) is returned.
Technique and why it applies: Two pointers exchange the outermost remaining vowels, which reverses their order while leaving skipped consonants untouched.
Invariant: The prefix and suffix outside [l,r] are finalized, and each swap places a pair of vowels in their reversed target positions.
Edge cases: Empty or vowel-free strings return equivalent content; a single vowel remains in place; indexOf tests the exact set "aeiouAEIOU", so accented vowels are not treated as vowels. Java strings are immutable, hence the char array is used for mutation.
Complexity: The pointer scans are O(n) time and the char array plus returned string require O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The pointers move monotonically through the char array, and converting to an array and constructing the returned String use linear space.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
notes:
Task and constraints: Return k values with highest frequencies from nums; the bucket approach groups distinct values by their counts and scans counts downward.
Idea: Counter builds frequencies, buckets has len(nums)+1 lists, and each value is placed in the list indexed by its count. The descending scan appends values until out has k elements, then returns early.
Technique and why it applies: Frequency buckets avoid sorting all distinct values by ordering groups directly by integer frequency, which cannot exceed the input length.
Invariant: Every distinct value is stored in exactly one bucket matching its count, and out contains values collected from higher frequencies before lower ones.
Edge cases: Empty input yields an empty output; k equal to the number of distinct values returns them all; ties within one bucket follow Counter iteration order and are not explicitly sorted.
Complexity: Counting, bucketing, and scanning the bucket array take O(n) time overall; the counter and buckets use O(n) space.
complexity_reason: Each input value is counted and placed in one frequency bucket, and the bucket array and output hold at most O(n) elements.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
notes:
Task and constraints: Select k most frequent integers from nums; frequencies are bounded by nums.length, allowing a bucket array instead of sorting distinct values.
Idea: A HashMap counts each integer. Each distinct key is placed in buckets[f], then buckets are traversed from highest frequency down to fill out until p reaches k.
Technique and why it applies: Bucket grouping makes frequency order explicit and avoids a comparison sort; the map handles arbitrary integer values.
Invariant: Every key occurs in the bucket matching its map count, and out is filled only from buckets in nonincreasing frequency order.
Edge cases: k=1 stops after the first emitted value; equal-frequency values have unspecified within-bucket order; the method assumes k is valid and returns an int array of exactly k entries. The generic List array may cause an unchecked warning but does not change the algorithm.
Complexity: Counting and bucketing are O(n) expected time, as is the descending scan; map, bucket array, and output use O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The map counts n inputs, each distinct key is inserted into one bucket, and the bucket scan covers at most n frequency slots.

title: Intersection of Two Arrays
notes:
Task and constraints: Return distinct integers present in both input arrays; duplicates in either input should not appear multiple times in the result.
Idea: The expression converts each array to a set, intersects the two sets with &, and converts the result back to a list.
Technique and why it applies: Hash-set intersection removes duplicates automatically and tests membership in expected constant time per value.
Invariant: Each set represents exactly the distinct values from its corresponding input, so their intersection contains precisely values shared by both arrays.
Edge cases: If either input is empty, the result is empty; repeated values appear once; negative integers are handled like any other hashable integer. Output order is not guaranteed by the set operation.
Complexity: Constructing both sets and intersecting them takes O(n+m) expected time; the sets and returned list use O(n+m) space.
complexity_reason: The two input arrays are converted into sets and the intersection list is materialized, with storage proportional to the distinct input values.

title: Intersection of Two Arrays
notes:
Task and constraints: Return each integer shared by two arrays once, discarding duplicate occurrences from either input.
Idea: The method fills set a from nums1, scans nums2 and adds values found in a to set b, then copies b into an int array sized to b.size().
Technique and why it applies: Hash sets provide expected constant-time membership and uniqueness, directly implementing a distinct intersection.
Invariant: a contains all distinct values from nums1, while b contains only values encountered in nums2 that also belong to a, without duplicates.
Edge cases: An empty input produces an empty array; repeated matches in nums2 are added to b once; HashSet iteration does not guarantee result order. The output index increments exactly once per distinct intersection member.
Complexity: Building and scanning sets takes O(n+m) expected time; the sets and output array use O(n+m) space.
complexity_reason: The method inserts each first-array value once, scans the second array once, and stores distinct matches in a set before copying them.

title: Intersection of Two Arrays II
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the multiset intersection of two arrays, preserving each common value up to the minimum of its two frequencies.
Idea: Counter(nums1) records available copies. The scan of nums2 appends x only when counts[x]>0 and decrements that count after consuming one matching occurrence.
Technique and why it applies: Frequency counting preserves multiplicity, unlike a set intersection, and consuming counts prevents any occurrence from being reused more than once.
Invariant: counts[x] is the number of unused occurrences of x from nums1; every appended value consumes exactly one such occurrence.
Edge cases: Empty arrays return an empty list; duplicates are emitted only as many times as available in both inputs; scanning nums2 controls the result order. Counter returns zero for missing keys.
Complexity: Counting nums1 and scanning nums2 take O(n+m) expected time; the counter stores at most n distinct keys, so auxiliary space is O(n).
complexity_reason: The first array is counted once and the second is scanned once; the counter stores at most one entry per distinct first-array value.

title: Intersection of Two Arrays II
notes:
Task and constraints: Compute the multiset intersection, returning common values no more often than their occurrence counts in either int array.
Idea: A HashMap counts nums1. The scan of nums2 checks each value's remaining count; positive counts append to tmp and decrement the map entry. Arrays.copyOf trims the temporary buffer to p matches.
Technique and why it applies: A frequency map tracks how many copies remain available, preserving duplicates while ensuring each first-array occurrence is consumed at most once.
Invariant: c[x] equals the unconsumed count of x from nums1, and tmp[0..p) contains exactly the matches found so far in nums2 order.
Edge cases: If either array is empty, p remains zero; duplicate values are returned up to the smaller frequency; tmp is sized to the shorter array, so p cannot exceed its capacity. Integer counts cannot exceed array length.
Complexity: Counting and scanning take O(n+m) expected time; the map and temporary/output arrays use O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The map counts the first array, the second array is scanned once, and the temporary array is no longer than the shorter input.
